title: A Reshuffle of Thirty-Five
statement:
Let $N$ be the number of permutations $\sigma$ of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, 35\}$ such that, for all distinct $i, j \in \{1, 2, \dots, 35\}$,
$$\gcd\bigl(|\sigma(i) - \sigma(j)|, 35\bigr) = 1 \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \gcd(|i - j|, 35) = 1.$$
Find the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$.
hints: Replace each number $i$ by the pair ($i$ mod $5$, $i$ mod $7$). Work out what the condition $\gcd(|i - j|, 35) = 1$ says about the pairs belonging to $i$ and $j$.

Model this as a graph: the vertices are the pairs of residues, and two vertices are joined when $\gcd(|i - j|, 35) = 1$, that is, when they differ in both coordinates. Then $\sigma$ is a graph automorphism, so it preserves the number of common neighbours of any two vertices. Compute this number for each way two distinct vertices can be related.

Two distinct vertices have $20$ common neighbours if they agree only mod $5$, $18$ if they agree only mod $7$, and $15$ if they agree in neither coordinate. So $\sigma$ preserves both congruence relations, and it acts by a permutation of the residues mod $5$ and, independently, by a permutation of the residues mod $7$. Check that every such pair of permutations gives a valid $\sigma$, then count the pairs.
solution: By the Chinese remainder theorem, $i \mapsto (i \bmod 5,\ i \bmod 7)$ is a bijection from $\{1, 2, \dots, 35\}$ to $\mathbb{Z}_5 \times \mathbb{Z}_7$. For distinct $i, j$, we have $\gcd(|i - j|, 35) = 1$ exactly when $5 \nmid i - j$ and $7 \nmid i - j$. So form a graph on these $35$ vertices, joining $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ when $a \ne c$ and $b \ne d$. The condition says that $\sigma$ sends adjacent pairs to adjacent pairs and non-adjacent pairs to non-adjacent pairs, so $\sigma$ is an automorphism of this graph. Consider two distinct vertices $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$. A common neighbour $(x, y)$ must satisfy $x \notin \{a, c\}$ and $y \notin \{b, d\}$, so there are three cases: If $a = c$ and $b \ne d$, there are $4 \cdot 5 = 20$ common neighbours. If $a \ne c$ and $b = d$, there are $3 \cdot 6 = 18$ common neighbours. If $a \ne c$ and $b \ne d$, there are $3 \cdot 5 = 15$ common neighbours. An automorphism maps the common neighbours of $u, v$ bijectively onto those of $\sigma(u), \sigma(v)$, so it preserves this count. Since $20$, $18$ and $15$ are different, for distinct $u, v$ we get $u \equiv v \pmod 5$ if and only if $\sigma(u) \equiv \sigma(v) \pmod 5$, and likewise mod $7$. Hence the residue of $\sigma(u)$ mod $5$ depends only on the residue of $u$ mod $5$, which gives a map $\alpha : \mathbb{Z}_5 \to \mathbb{Z}_5$. The "only if" direction above makes $\alpha$ injective, so it is a permutation. In the same way we get a permutation $\beta$ of $\mathbb{Z}_7$, and $\sigma(a, b) = (\alpha(a), \beta(b))$. Conversely, take any permutations $\alpha$ of $\mathbb{Z}_5$ and $\beta$ of $\mathbb{Z}_7$. The map $(a, b) \mapsto (\alpha(a), \beta(b))$ is a bijection of the vertices. Also $a \ne c$ and $b \ne d$ hold exactly when $\alpha(a) \ne \alpha(c)$ and $\beta(b) \ne \beta(d)$, so the map satisfies the condition. Different pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ give different maps, so valid permutations $\sigma$ correspond one-to-one with pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$. Therefore $N = 5! \cdot 7! = 120 \cdot 5040 = 604800$, and the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$ is $800$. Why this works. graph-modeling, crt, rule-of-product: in the graph on residue pairs, common-neighbour counts reveal which coordinate two vertices share, so $\sigma$ splits into independent permutations of the two coordinates, whose counts multiply.
